items.prompt: Which term names the sequence of events in a story, from setup through rising tension and climax to resolution?

options.label: Point of view
Tone of voice
Word count
Story arc

rubric: The story arc is the shape of events from beginning to end.
Point of view and tone describe how the story is told, not its event sequence.

items.prompt: What is the climax of a story?

options.label: The closing lines where the story wraps up and the lesson is summarised
The point of highest tension where the conflict comes to a head
The opening scene that introduces the setting and the main characters
The background given about a minor character to explain their motives

rubric: The climax is the peak of tension and the turning point of the conflict.
Opening and closing parts are exposition and resolution.

items.prompt: What is the protagonist of a story?

options.label: The narrator who tells the story to its audience
The main character whose goal drives the plot
The audience member the story is told to reach
The opposing force or person who blocks the hero

rubric: The protagonist is the central character pursuing a goal.
The opposing force is the antagonist; the narrator is not always the protagonist.

items.prompt: Which part of a story usually comes first in a classic structure?

options.label: Resolution
Exposition
Climax
Falling action

rubric: Exposition sets up characters and setting at the start.
Climax, falling action and resolution come later.

items.prompt: What does 'conflict' mean in storytelling?

options.label: A disagreement between the storyteller and the audience
A struggle between a character and an obstacle or opponent
A moment when the story pauses to describe the setting
A twist at the end that changes what the audience believed

rubric: Conflict is the struggle that creates tension and drives the plot.
It is not an error or an audience dispute.

items.prompt: Which of the following are core elements of a story? Select all that apply.

options.label: Setting
Footnotes
Table of contents
Plot events
Character

rubric: Characters, plot events and setting are core story elements.
Footnotes and a table of contents are formatting features of documents.

items.prompt: A new speaker is planning a talk. Her coach says, 'Begin with exposition, then build rising action, reach the climax, and finish with the resolution.' She wants to recall the name for the final part, where loose ends are tied up after the peak. What is it called?

options.label: Rising action
Inciting incident
Resolution
Exposition

rubric: The resolution ties up the story after the climax.
The inciting incident and exposition come early; rising action precedes the climax.

items.prompt: Why do storytellers add obstacles for the main character?

options.label: To create tension that keeps the audience wondering what happens
To delay the ending so the story runs long enough to feel complete
To show the audience how much the narrator knows about the setting
To give the audience time to forget the main character's goal

rubric: Obstacles create tension and make the goal feel earned.
Length or facts are not the purpose; stories need a climax.

items.prompt: A speaker says 'Sales rose 12%' versus telling about one customer whose shop was saved by the product. Why does the second version often engage an audience more?

options.label: Statistics are less reliable than a single anecdote, so listeners discount them
A longer talk signals more effort, so listeners tend to give it more attention
Stories are mostly about entertainment, so listeners relax and stop judging claims
A named person facing a problem lets listeners feel and care

rubric: Characters in a struggle create emotional connection.
Data is not inherently wrong, and length is not the cause.

items.prompt: Which opening is an example of starting in the middle of the action?

options.label: 'Before I begin, let me explain the history of this town.'
'This story has three parts, and I will cover each in order.'
'Stories matter because people have always used them to learn.'
'The alarm was already blaring when Maya reached the door.'

rubric: It drops the listener into a moment of tension.
The others are background, outlines or generalities.

items.prompt: What is the difference between 'showing' and 'telling' in writing?

options.label: Showing keeps the narrator out of the scene; telling brings characters in
Showing uses longer, more elaborate sentences; telling uses brief ones
Showing uses concrete details and actions; telling states conclusions
Showing is for spoken stories, while telling is for written stories

rubric: Showing lets readers infer feelings from details.
The distinction is not about medium or sentence length.

items.prompt: A story has a hero, a goal and a big problem, but ends right at the climax with no further events. What is most likely missing?

options.label: A new protagonist to carry the story forward
A second climax that raises the tension higher
A resolution showing the outcome
More exposition about the setting and backstory

rubric: The resolution gives closure after the peak.
Adding other elements does not fix the missing ending.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why a clear arc helps an audience? Select all that apply.

options.label: It gives listeners a sense of direction through the events
It guarantees agreement from every listener
It builds anticipation toward a payoff
It makes the message easier to remember
It lets the speaker skip the characters

rubric: Arcs give direction, anticipation and memorability.
They don't replace characters or guarantee agreement.

items.prompt: A manager tells her team about a failed project. She begins with the team's confident plan, then describes the setbacks, the night they nearly quit, and finally what they learned. A colleague asks why she put the near-quitting moment late in the story. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Listeners remember best what they hear first, so she saved a minor detail for later
Placing the hardest moment late keeps the team from dwelling on the project's failure
Tension builds toward that low point, which makes the lesson that follows land harder
Stories hold attention better when the most emotional event comes after the lesson

rubric: The low point is the peak of tension that gives the resolution weight.
The other options misread the purpose of tension.

items.prompt: In a story, what is the main job of the inciting incident?

options.label: It reveals the ending early so the audience knows how things turn out
It resolves the central conflict and sends the character back home
It introduces every minor character before any of the plot begins
It disrupts the character's normal life and starts the main problem

rubric: The inciting incident breaks the status quo and launches the central problem.
Distractors confuse it with a spoiler, the resolution, or the setup.

items.prompt: Why do stakes matter in a story?

options.label: They list the facts of the setting so the audience can follow along
They promise a happy ending so the audience feels safe and satisfied
They show what the character could win or lose, so the audience cares
They slow the pace so listeners can rest between the scenes

rubric: Stakes give the audience a reason to care about the outcome.
Distractors mistake stakes for exposition, pacing or guaranteed endings.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows a character's nerves rather than simply telling the audience about them?

options.label: Maya pressed her damp palms to her knees and reread the same line twice.
Maya was the kind of person who got nervous in every situation.
Maya felt a great deal of anxiety about the big interview ahead.
Maya was so nervous before the interview that she could hardly think.

rubric: Showing uses concrete actions and details that let the audience infer the feeling.
The other options name the emotion directly, which is telling.

items.prompt: Which best describes a story's theme, as distinct from its plot?

options.label: The setting in time and place where the events unfold for the audience
The order of events from the opening scene to the final scene
The list of characters who take part in the main events of the story
The underlying idea about life that the events explore

rubric: Theme is the underlying idea; plot is the sequence of events.
Distractors describe plot, setting and cast instead.

items.prompt: A draft has a hero who wants a goal and reaches it at once, with no setbacks. What is the likely effect on the audience?

options.label: The story feels longer because the goal is reached early in the telling
Tension stays low because nothing stands between the hero and the goal
The audience bonds more with the hero because the hero seems very competent
Suspense rises because success seems certain and everyone waits for it

rubric: Without obstacles there is no conflict, so tension and interest stay low.
Distractors wrongly treat easy success as suspense, connection or length.

items.prompt: Which techniques build tension in a story? Select all that apply.

options.label: Stating the final outcome in the first sentence
Delaying the answer to a question the audience cares about
Adding an obstacle that makes the goal harder to reach
Spending several paragraphs on background facts before anything happens
Raising what the character stands to lose

rubric: Delayed answers, rising stakes and obstacles all increase tension.
Giving away the outcome or front-loading background releases or avoids tension.

items.prompt: A manager opens a safety talk with three injury statistics and the room drifts off. She then describes one coworker, Luis, who slipped on a wet floor and missed his daughter's recital, and everyone listens closely. Why did the second approach work better?

options.label: A single short example is easier to remember than three statistics, so listeners stayed focused on it
The story added a lighter, more personal tone, which relaxed the room so listeners paid closer attention
The statistics were too general to be believed, so one verified incident gave the room more reliable evidence
A specific person with something at stake lets listeners feel the problem, not just hear it

rubric: A concrete character with stakes creates emotional engagement that numbers alone do not.
Distractors invent reasons about length, accuracy or humour that the situation does not support.

items.prompt: Dev wants to win a cooking contest, faces a rival, loses his key ingredient, and wins the final round with a daring substitute. Which beat should come next in a standard arc?

options.label: A long backstory about Dev's childhood to explain his cooking style
A new inciting incident that restarts the contest from the beginning
A brief resolution showing how Dev's life is changed by the win
Another rising obstacle that is bigger than the final round was

rubric: After the climax, a short resolution shows the aftermath and change.
Distractors restart, backtrack or escalate after the story's peak.

items.prompt: Which rewrite best turns the telling line 'The old shop was run-down' into showing?

options.label: The shop looked terrible, as if nobody had cared for it in years.
Paint curled off the sign; one bulb buzzed over dusty shelves.
The shop, which was run-down, sat at the far end of a quiet street.
The shop was very old and shabby, and it was in a poor state of repair.

rubric: Concrete sensory details let the reader infer the run-down state.
The others restate the judgment with different adjectives.

items.prompt: You open a two-minute talk on why your team needs a new ordering tool. Which opening best applies a story hook?

options.label: Good evening. Today I will talk about our ordering tool, how it works and which features it offers.
Let me begin by thanking everyone for coming and for giving up their time on such a busy evening.
Last Tuesday at 2 a.m., Priya was still re-entering orders by hand when the system froze.
Studies of small teams show that manual data entry has several well-known drawbacks, including slow and error-prone work.

rubric: A specific character, moment and problem pulls the audience in at once.
The others are announcements, general claims or pleasantries, not story hooks.

items.prompt: You have four beats: A) Sam is fired; B) Sam starts a bakery; C) Sam's oven breaks the night before a big order; D) Sam delivers the order and opens a second shop. Which order fits a clear story arc?

options.label: A, C, B, D
B, A, C, D
A, B, C, D
C, A, B, D

rubric: The firing triggers the goal, the bakery starts the pursuit, the broken oven is the crisis, and the delivery resolves it.
Other orders break cause and effect, such as the crisis arriving before the bakery exists.

items.prompt: A pitch says, 'Our team wants to build a community garden.' Which revision best adds stakes?

options.label: Our team has built three gardens before and has years of experience in community projects.
Community gardens are popular in many cities and have grown fast in the last ten years.
Our team wants to build a very beautiful, colorful community garden here this year.
Without it, Mrs. Ortiz's street loses its only shared space by June.

rubric: Stakes name a person, a possible loss and a deadline.
The others add decoration, general facts or credentials, but no loss.

items.prompt: You must cut a 10-minute story to 5 minutes without losing its arc. Which edits would you make? Select all that apply.

options.label: Remove a side character whose scene does not change the main problem
Trim description that affects neither events nor emotion
Keep the inciting incident, the climax and the resolution
Cut the climax because it takes the most time to tell
Cut the obstacle scenes so the hero reaches the goal sooner

rubric: Cutting non-essential scenes and description while keeping the key beats preserves the arc.
Cutting the climax or obstacles removes the tension the arc depends on.

items.prompt: Jon wants his team to adopt code review. He has one real episode: a skipped review let a bug reach customers, he stayed up fixing it, and a later review caught a similar bug early. How should he structure the story for the talk?

options.label: Tell the episode in random order so listeners piece the meaning together
Describe the team's tools first, then the bug, and end on the general rule
Start with the bug and what it cost, show the night of fixing, then end with the early catch
Begin with the happy ending, then list every review rule, and skip the night of fixing

rubric: A clear arc moves from problem and stakes through struggle to a resolution that supports the point.
Distractors bury the conflict, lead with tools or rules, or scramble the order.

items.prompt: You have 3 minutes to persuade a town council to fund a crosswalk. You have a true anecdote about a child's near-miss. Which structure best applies a story arc to the talk?

options.label: Describe the street's history first, then give the data, and tell the anecdote after the ask
Open with the near-miss moment, widen to the data, then return to the child as you make the ask
Tell the anecdote in full, then list five other safety projects so the council can compare costs
Open with the statistics, then close by briefly mentioning that a child was nearly hit once

rubric: Opening on the tense moment, widening to evidence and returning to the character gives a clear arc ending in the ask.
Distractors bury the anecdote or dilute it, so the tension never builds or pays off.

items.prompt: You are revising the line "Maria was nervous" in a short story. Which rewrite best applies the 'show, don't tell' technique?

options.label: Maria pressed her thumbnail into her palm and read the same line of the form three times
Maria was so anxious that she thought she might be sick before her name was called
Maria's nervousness was obvious to everyone in the waiting room as they watched her
Maria felt a wave of nervousness wash over her as she sat waiting for her name

rubric: Concrete behaviour lets the audience infer the emotion instead of being told it.
Other options name the feeling or restate it with stronger adjectives, which is still telling.

items.prompt: In a story, Dana is hiking to a summit before dark to scatter her father's ashes. The draft feels flat. Which single addition best raises the tension?

options.label: A paragraph describing in detail how beautiful the valley looks in the afternoon light
A narrator comment reminding readers that the hike is very important to Dana's family
A flashback explaining how Dana and her father first met their favourite hiking group
A storm moving in, with a turnaround time Dana knows she will miss if she keeps going

rubric: A ticking clock and a real choice put the protagonist's goal at risk, which raises stakes.
Other options add description, backstory or telling without adding any obstacle or risk.

items.prompt: You are writing a story where the reader should slowly realise the narrator's brother is lying, without being told. Which narration choice best fits?

options.label: A second-person narrator addressing the brother directly about each of his lies
An omniscient narrator who states early on that the brother has hidden motives
A first-person narrator who announces at the start that she was later betrayed by him
A first-person narrator who trusts her brother and reports details she doesn't yet question

rubric: A trusting, limited narrator lets clues surface that readers can interpret before she does.
The other choices reveal the lie up front, which removes the discovery.

items.prompt: You tell a 5-minute story at a networking event, but 4 minutes go on the narrator's childhood before the main event. Which edit best applies good pacing?

options.label: Keep every backstory detail, but speed up your speaking so the main event gets more time
Add a second backstory anecdote so listeners care about the narrator before the event happens
Move the main event to the start and cut all backstory so the story has no setup
Trim backstory to the details that explain the later choice, and begin close to the inciting event

rubric: Keep only the setup that the later choice depends on and start near the trigger.
Distractors keep the imbalance, remove needed context, or add even more setup.

items.prompt: You are turning a customer success case into a story for a sales deck. Which edits apply the principle of giving the protagonist a clear want and an obstacle? Select all that apply.

options.label: Show the customer making the decision that turned things around
State what the customer needed to achieve by a specific date
Show a first attempt that failed and what it cost the customer
Open with a slide listing the product's twelve main features
Describe the product as the hero who arrives to save the day

rubric: A clear goal, a costly obstacle and an active decision are the core of a want-obstacle-choice arc.
Feature lists and a product-as-hero framing take the protagonist role away from the customer.

items.prompt: A science teacher wants to explain how a vaccine trains the immune system to a class of 12-year-olds using a story. She has a plan: a castle with guards who have never seen a particular invader. Which next step best applies story structure?

options.label: Describe the guards' armour and the castle's layout in rich detail before any invader appears, so students can picture the setting
Have the guards defeat the invader immediately so the explanation stays simple and the students are not confused by any struggle
Have the invader arrive, the guards fail at first, then get a 'wanted poster' so they win quickly next time
Tell the class the story's moral first, then narrate the castle scenes one by one to illustrate each point of the moral

rubric: A problem, a struggle and a resolution that mirrors the mechanism lets the arc carry the explanation.
Distractors delay the conflict, state the moral first, or remove conflict entirely.

items.prompt: A listener says your 6-minute story "lost me in the middle." The middle has three scenes, each showing the protagonist failing to reach a client with the same unreturned call. What is the most likely structural cause?

options.label: The protagonist is too sympathetic, which removes any suspense about the outcome entirely
The middle repeats one complication three times instead of escalating with new obstacles
The ending is too short to resolve everything the listener has been told about the client
The opening hook is too weak, so the audience never became interested in the protagonist

rubric: Repeating the same obstacle without escalation stalls momentum in the middle.
The other causes are not supported by the described problem, which is about the middle's content.

items.prompt: In a draft, a stranded sailor gives up, then a passing ship happens to find him. Readers say the ending feels unearned. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The rescue arrives too late in the story, so readers have already lost interest in whether he survives
The rescue comes from coincidence, not the sailor's choices, so the climax doesn't pay off his arc
The sailor is described too sparsely, so readers can't picture him or feel invested when he is saved
The ending is too happy for the tone set earlier, so a tragic ending would feel more earned here

rubric: Resolution by outside luck disconnects the climax from the character's decisions.
Timing, description and tone are not the cause; a rescue can be earned if the protagonist's actions lead to it.

items.prompt: A nonprofit director tells a donor story about herself: the crisis she spotted, the plan she made, the work she did. Donors admire her but give little. Which analysis best explains why?

options.label: The story opens with a crisis, which makes donors feel anxious and helpless, so they avoid the issue and withhold gifts
The story is too specific to one person's experience, and donors respond better to general claims about the cause's scale
The story is told in first person, which weakens persuasion because donors distrust speakers who talk about themselves
The story casts the speaker as hero, so donors have no role in it and no reason to see themselves in it

rubric: Persuasive stories usually give the audience a part to play, such as enabling the hero.
Crisis, first person and specificity are not inherently flawed; the issue is who the story is about.

items.prompt: A character in your novel always does the right thing, and readers call her flat. She wants to win a promotion, and no choice she makes ever costs her anything. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: She needs a longer backstory, because readers connect through knowing everything about her past
Her choices carry no cost or conflict of values, so they never reveal who she is under pressure
She needs a funnier voice, because likeability comes mainly from humour in dialogue
She needs more physical description, because readers cannot picture her clearly enough

rubric: Character is revealed through choices under pressure, which requires real cost or competing values.
Description, humour and backstory do not fix the lack of meaningful choices.

items.prompt: Readers of your mystery say the twist, that the gardener did it, feels like a cheat. In the draft the gardener appears once in chapter 1 and again in the last chapter. Which analysis is best?

options.label: The twist comes too close to the end, so the reveal should move to the midpoint of the book
The twist is too surprising, so the culprit should be guessable by readers early in the story
The gardener is too minor a character, so the culprit should be someone central to the plot
The twist has no planted clues, so the reveal can't feel inevitable in hindsight

rubric: Good twists feel surprising but inevitable because earlier clues were planted.
The other options misdiagnose by demanding predictability, a specific culprit or a fixed reveal point.

items.prompt: A short story's protagonist wants to win a regional chess final, but readers report low tension throughout. Which observations would explain the problem? Select all that apply.

options.label: Every game in the story ends in an easy win for her
Nothing is at risk if she loses, as the story never says why the win matters
Her opponent is never shown and has no visible strengths
The story includes a scene describing the tournament hall
The narration is in the past tense

rubric: Tension needs a capable opposing force, real stakes and a chance of failure.
Setting description and tense are neutral and don't remove tension.

items.prompt: A manager tells the all-hands a turnaround story: "We had a revenue problem, we had a vision, and now we are thriving." Staff reaction is cynical. Several say it feels like spin. Which analysis best explains the reaction?

options.label: The story skips the low point and hard choices, so the success feels unearned
The story is too short for staff to absorb, since a turnaround needs a long telling to be believed
The story names a vision, which staff tend to hear as management jargon rather than a real plan
The story dwells on the revenue problem, which leaves staff doubting that the results are real

rubric: Without a visible low point, cost and difficult decisions, the jump from problem to success reads as spin.
Length, 'vision' and too much problem focus are not the main cause; omitted struggle is.

items.prompt: A founder's pitch story opens with ten minutes of company history, then reaches the customer's crisis in the last two minutes. Listeners say it felt flat, though every fact was vivid. What is the most likely structural cause?

options.label: The ending is too short, so listeners cannot tell who the protagonist of the story is
The stakes and conflict arrive too late, so early material has no tension to hold attention
The story lacks enough statistics, so listeners cannot judge whether the facts are credible
The customer's crisis is too dramatic, which overwhelms the earlier historical details

rubric: Tension needs a goal and stakes early; background without conflict reads as flat.
Distractors blame data or ending length rather than the delayed conflict.

items.prompt: In a short story, the narrator announces 'she was deeply lonely' and then describes her evening. Readers feel distant from her. Which analysis best explains why?

options.label: The narrator names only a single emotion, so readers lack the range of feelings they need to build a connection with her
The story is told in third person, which keeps readers outside her thoughts and so limits how much they can feel for her
The loneliness is stated, not dramatised, so readers get a conclusion instead of evidence to infer it from
The evening is described in too much sensory detail, which crowds out her feelings and leaves readers unsure how she feels

rubric: Telling a conclusion bypasses the reader's own inference; concrete behaviour creates feeling.
Distractors blame detail, person or emotion count, none of which is the cause.

items.prompt: A speaker tells a story in which the hero succeeds on the first attempt with no obstacles, then draws a lesson about perseverance. Why does the lesson fail to land?

options.label: The plot shows no struggle, so the stated lesson contradicts the events
The hero is too competent, so audiences tend to distrust lessons from characters who never show flaws
The lesson is stated outright at the end, which weakens a moral that works better when left implied
The story is too short to build the emotional investment that a lesson usually needs to be believed

rubric: Theme must be carried by events; an obstacle-free plot cannot show perseverance.
Distractors offer generic rules about flaws, length or unspoken morals.

items.prompt: A memoir chapter jumps between 1998, 2015 and 2003 without signals. Beta readers say they lost the emotional thread, though each scene works alone. Which diagnosis is most precise?

options.label: No causal or thematic logic links the jumps, so readers can't tell why each scene follows the last
The scenes are individually so strong that they compete for attention, so each one dilutes the impact of the others
Nonlinear order is inherently confusing to readers, so chronology is the only structure that can carry emotion
The chapter has too many people across the three periods, so cutting a character would repair the thread

rubric: Nonlinear structure works when a thematic or causal link justifies each jump.
Distractors blame scene strength, nonlinearity itself or character count.

items.prompt: A manager's change-management story casts the company as a hero who overcame a villain, 'resistant staff'. Staff in the audience grow hostile. What explains the reaction?

options.label: The villain is described too vaguely, so staff cannot tell what the hero actually overcame in the story
The audience is cast as the antagonist, so the story invites them to side against themselves
The hero's victories are too few, so staff doubt the company can succeed with the change
The story runs too long, so staff lose patience before the resolution of the arc arrives

rubric: Audiences identify with a role in the story; being cast as the villain provokes defensiveness.
Distractors address detail, length or victories rather than audience positioning.

items.prompt: A tense chase scene in a thriller reads slowly. The paragraphs are long, with reflective asides about the hero's childhood and complex subordinate clauses. Which analyses identify real contributors to the lost pace? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reflective interior material suits calmer moments and works against urgency here
Close focus on the hero's immediate goal narrows the scene and drains its suspense
Long sentences with nested clauses slow the reading rhythm that should feel rapid
Dense description of each location slows the chase, so the setting should be cut entirely

items.prompt: A nonprofit director tells donors about a girl named Amina who overcame hardship thanks to a scholarship. Donors say they were moved but cannot say what their gift would change. The story ends on Amina's graduation, with no mention of the programme's next steps. What is the main structural gap?

options.label: Amina's path has so many emotional beats in a row that donors lose the thread of her progress and cannot tell which moment mattered most
The story rests on one individual, and donors need aggregate statistics instead of a single character to judge what a gift achieves
The graduation scene comes too late in the telling, so donors' attention fades before the point and an earlier ending would raise giving
The resolution closes the arc without tying donors' action to a future need, so no call to act emerges from the story

rubric: A persuasive story must connect its resolution to the audience's possible role.
Distractors suggest dropping character or reordering without addressing the missing link.

items.prompt: You must explain a complex data-privacy policy to 200 employees in five minutes, and the goal is behaviour change. Which approach best meets that goal and time limit?

options.label: Narrate one realistic employee's mistake and its consequences, then show the one habit that would have prevented it
Walk through every clause in order so nothing is omitted, then invite questions on any section that employees found unclear afterwards
Open with a vivid personal anecdote about your own career to build rapport, then summarise the main rules in a closing slide of bullets
Present a timeline of how the policy was drafted and reviewed, so employees trust its rigour and feel obliged to follow what it says

rubric: A focused case with consequence and a single actionable habit fits time and behavioural aims.
Distractors prioritise completeness, rapport or history over the goal.

items.prompt: Criteria: the audience must trust the speaker and remember one point. Which opening for a talk on workplace safety best satisfies both?

options.label: A brief account of the speaker's own near-miss, ending on the one rule that would have prevented it
A quote from a famous author on the value of caution, followed by the agenda
A joke unrelated to safety, to relax the room before the content begins
A list of accident statistics from the past decade, followed by an apology for the grim topic

rubric: A personal, specific story builds credibility and anchors one memorable rule.
Distractors are impersonal, scattered or unrelated to the single point.

items.prompt: A writer's twist ending reveals the narrator was dead all along. Criteria: the twist should feel earned, not cheap. Which draft revision best meets the criteria?

options.label: Have the narrator say several times that they are alive and well, so readers are firmly misdirected before the reveal
Remove every earlier hint about the narrator's state, so the reveal lands as a complete surprise with nothing to anticipate
Plant early details, like unanswered greetings and untouched objects, that gain new meaning on rereading
Add a closing paragraph in which another character explains step by step how the narrator died and why

rubric: Earned twists rely on fair clues that recast earlier scenes.
Total surprise or explanation feels arbitrary; false statements break trust.

items.prompt: A trainer compares two versions of a case story for new nurses. Version A is chronological with every detail. Version B opens at the moment of the error, then backtracks to its causes. Criterion: learners must grasp why the error happened. Which judgement is best supported?

options.label: Version A, because starting with the error would frighten learners and reduce their attention to the causes that follow
Neither, because causal reasoning cannot be taught through any narrative form
Version A, because a full chronology lets learners see every detail and so reach the causes unaided
Version B, because opening on the outcome frames the causal questions that the backtracking answers

rubric: Opening on the outcome creates a question that the causal backtracking resolves.
Distractors assume completeness or fear, or deny narrative's teaching role.

items.prompt: Two endings for a corporate turnaround story: (1) 'And we have never faced difficulty since.' (2) 'The crisis is over, but the habits that caused it still need guarding.' Criteria: credibility with sceptical staff and an honest message. Which is better, and why?

options.label: Ending 1, because acknowledging remaining risk would weaken the turnaround narrative
Ending 1, because a fully positive close inspires the most confidence in sceptical listeners
Ending 2, because a closing note of unresolved tension keeps listeners engaged and attentive afterwards
Ending 2, because admitting unfinished work keeps the story credible and gives staff a role

rubric: Sceptical audiences distrust tidy triumph; honest unfinished business is credible.
Distractors favour spin or misstate the reason for ambiguity.

items.prompt: A speaker must pick a protagonist for a fundraising story. Criteria: the audience should identify with the character and see a realistic route to change. Which choices fit these criteria? Select all that apply.

options.label: An institution described only through its mission statement and annual figures
A composite hero with extraordinary powers, so that the audience admires but cannot relate
A specific individual with a clear want and a concrete obstacle the audience could help remove
A person whose situation resembles the audience's own values and everyday concerns

rubric: Identification and an actionable obstacle require a specific, relatable person.
Superheroes and institutions block identification.

items.prompt: A founder has three minutes to pitch investors. Draft A tells her own struggle for two minutes, then states the product. Draft B opens with the customer's problem, shows the product resolving it in a short scene, then mentions her background in one line. Investors' criterion: is there a real, large problem with a credible solution? Which draft is better?

options.label: Draft A, because a founder's personal struggle builds more trust and emotional pull than a product scene
Draft B, because it spends the time on the problem and solution the criterion tests
Draft B, because a scene with a customer is more entertaining than a founder's own story
Draft A, because investors back the person, so more time on her story shows credibility

rubric: Time should go to the evidence the audience's criterion requires.
Distractors use absolute claims about investors or ordering.

items.prompt: You have five minutes to persuade sceptical engineers to adopt a safety checklist. Criteria: credibility with doubters, brevity, emotional pull without manipulation. Which opening is best?

options.label: Open with a rhetorical question about safety, then walk through all twelve checklist steps in order to build the logical case.
Open with a near-miss from their own team told in concrete detail, then show the one checklist step that would have caught it.
Open with a general statistic on industry accident rates, then close with a sentimental anecdote about a victim's grieving family.
Open with a dramatic rescue from another industry, then link it to their own work through an analogy in the final minute.

rubric: A near-miss from their own team is credible and concrete, and ties the checklist directly to the story's turning point.
Distractors rely on generic statistics, sentiment, a step list, or a distant analogy, none of which earns trust from sceptics.

items.prompt: A case study meant to teach resilience shows its founder solving every crisis smoothly and without cost. Judged against the aim of teaching how to decide under pressure, which critique is strongest?

options.label: The story lacks a stated moral, so listeners will not know which lesson the founder wants them to take away from it.
The story should be retold in strict chronological order, since the smooth sequence of crises hides the underlying causes.
The cast is too small, because several competing characters would add the conflict that makes any narrative persuasive.
Without real setbacks or costs the stakes never register, so listeners cannot see what each decision weighed or risked.

rubric: Without cost or setback there is no tension, so the decision-making under pressure is invisible to the audience.
Distractors blame missing morals, ordering or cast size, which do not address the absent stakes.

items.prompt: A thriller could reveal the detective's driving backstory in chapter 1 or withhold it. Criteria: sustain tension through the middle, and make the climactic choice feel earned. Which placement is best?

options.label: Spread the full backstory evenly across flashbacks in every chapter so readers never feel any gap in what they know.
Seed hints early and reveal it just before the climax, so the middle holds a question and the final choice lands.
Withhold it entirely until the epilogue, since explaining the motive after the climax preserves maximum mystery to the very end.
Reveal it fully in chapter 1 so readers understand the motive from the start and every later scene gains emotional weight.

rubric: Early hints open a question, and the late reveal explains the climactic choice at the moment it matters.
Distractors either spend the mystery too early, withhold the meaning until after the climax, or remove any open question.

items.prompt: A consultant presents a composite customer as a real named person in a talk meant to persuade a sceptical board. Ranking risks to the persuasive aim, which is greatest?

options.label: The composite will seem less vivid than a real case, so the board will feel only mild emotion and will recall little afterward.
A composite has no clear want or obstacle of its own, so the board cannot follow the arc that the recommendation depends upon.
If the composite is exposed, doubt spreads to every claim in the talk, so the board discounts the evidence along with the story.
The story will run longer than a real case study would, so board members will lose focus before the recommendation is reached.

rubric: Exposed fabrication damages trust in the whole talk, which is fatal for a sceptical audience.
Distractors name craft weaknesses that are not inherent to composites and are far smaller than a loss of credibility.

items.prompt: A founder tells the story of a failed launch to teach a team. Criteria: honest about uncertainty, avoids hindsight bias, keeps listeners engaged. Which narration choice fits best?

options.label: Narrate each decision with only what was known at that moment, then pause to name what later information changed.
Narrate as an outside observer who lists the errors briefly, so the founder's emotions cannot distort the facts told.
Narrate only the final failure in vivid detail, leaving earlier decisions out so that the climax carries all the attention.
Narrate in the voice of the founder's present knowledge, explaining each error as obviously avoidable so the lesson is plain.

rubric: Telling decisions from the knowledge available then keeps uncertainty real and avoids hindsight bias, while keeping suspense.
Distractors use hindsight, remove the human stakes, or omit the decisions that carry the lesson.

items.prompt: A storyteller considers breaking chronological order. Given the aim of holding attention and carrying meaning, which are sound reasons to do so? Select all that apply.

options.label: Opening at the crisis point lets listeners feel the stakes before a slow setup, which is then filled in as backstory.
Withholding a key outcome creates a question the audience wants answered, so later events are read with that question in mind.
Jumping around in time works better for every audience, because linear stories are always predictable and dull.
Reordering signals sophistication, so audiences credit the speaker with more skill even when the order adds nothing.
Reordering hides the causes of events, which spares the audience from having to follow the logic linking them.

rubric: Starting at the crisis and withholding an outcome both serve tension and meaning.
Distractors treat reordering as decoration, obscuring causes, or a universal rule.

items.prompt: A charity has four minutes to move donors at a gala. Draft A follows one child from need to a turning point and an uncertain future. Draft B names five children with a line each, plus totals. Donors decide emotionally and must picture results. Which draft is the better choice?

options.label: Draft B, because brief lines let listeners choose a favourite child, which increases their personal identification with the cause.
Draft A, because a single case avoids statistics entirely, and numbers always weaken emotional response in any audience.
Draft A, because one character with a clear want and obstacle builds tension and a picturable outcome within four minutes.
Draft B, because five cases show breadth and scale, and donors respond most strongly to the size of a problem.

rubric: One identifiable character with want, obstacle and turning point fits four minutes and gives donors an outcome to picture.
Distractors favour breadth or claim numbers always weaken emotion, which is an overgeneralisation.

items.prompt: Design the ending of a case study on ignored early warnings. Constraints: no villain, no individual blamed, listeners leave able to act. Which ending meets all three?

options.label: Close by praising the team's effort, then summarise the timeline neutrally so listeners can judge for themselves what went wrong.
Close when the signals were still visible, show the small routine check that would have caught them, and ask which listeners will adopt.
Close with a vivid account of the final disaster, then list what regulators later required of every company in the field.
Close on the manager's failure to read the reports, then state that the lesson is to pay closer attention to warnings.

rubric: It places blame on no one, and gives a concrete, adoptable action at the moment the signals mattered.
Distractors blame a person, lean on regulation instead of action, or leave listeners without a next step.

items.prompt: Plan a 90-second story explaining compound interest to teenagers. Constraints: one character, one visible change, one turning point, no jargon. Which plan meets all constraints?

options.label: Two friends save differently, one starting early and one late; the narrator then explains the formula behind the gap.
A teen saves £10 monthly and checks the balance often; the turning point is the month interest beats the deposit.
A teacher lectures on interest rates, then gives a worked example, and ends with the moral that patience always pays.
A teen saves £10 monthly and watches the balance climb steadily each month; the story ends on the final total with a reminder to start early.

rubric: One character, a visible balance change and a clear turning point where interest outgrows deposits.
Distractors use two characters, a lecture format, or omit a turning point.

items.prompt: A story sags in the middle. Constraints: keep the existing ending, add no length, keep the same protagonist. Which fix meets all three?

options.label: Trim the setup and place a midpoint reversal that forces the protagonist to choose, leading to the same ending.
Expand the descriptive passages in the middle so the setting feels richer and the pace slows to build deeper atmosphere.
Introduce a new antagonist at the midpoint whose arrival raises the stakes and gives the ending a fresh opposing force.
Add a subplot with a secondary character whose problem mirrors the protagonist's, giving the middle more incident and some variety.

rubric: Compressing setup frees space for a midpoint reversal, so length and ending stay fixed.
Distractors add length or change what the ending must resolve.

items.prompt: Craft a telling of a failed project for executives and frontline staff. Constraints: truthful, no blame on individuals, motivates future work. Which structure meets all three?

options.label: Make the failure the opening line, narrate a list of causes by department, and end on a call to work harder next time.
Make the project manager the protagonist, narrate the errors in order, and end on a candid apology delivered to the whole staff.
Make the market the antagonist, narrate how conditions shifted unexpectedly, and end on reassurance that nothing could have been done differently.
Make the shared goal the protagonist, narrate three decisions with what was known then, and end on what the team now does differently.

rubric: A shared-goal protagonist keeps it truthful and blameless while the ending turns the lesson into action.
Distractors blame a person or department, or deny any learning, which breaks a constraint.

items.prompt: A talk meant to get listeners to adopt a new habit has a hero, goal, obstacle, climax and resolution. What is the most important element the design is missing?

options.label: A bridge from the hero's case to the listener's own situation, with one concrete first action.
A longer backstory for the hero, because listeners must know the hero's history before they will trust the habit shown.
An ambiguous ending, because leaving the outcome open makes listeners more likely to supply their own conclusion and act.
A second antagonist, because a single obstacle makes the climax too easy and gives listeners nothing to compare against.

rubric: Persuasion into action needs a link from the story to the listener's life and a specific first step.
Distractors add story material or ambiguity without connecting to the listener's action.

items.prompt: Design a 2-minute spoken story, heard once, after which listeners must remember one idea. Which elements fit that design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Several statistics in the middle, because numbers give the story the credibility that makes it memorable.
Parallel subplots linked by callbacks, since a rich structure helps listeners retain the central idea.
One concrete image or phrase repeated at the key moments so the idea attaches to something memorable.
A single turning point that visibly carries the idea, with the rest of the story building toward it.

rubric: Repetition of one image and one clear turning point suit a single hearing and one idea.
Subplots and statistics overload a listener who cannot re-read.

items.prompt: A novelist's scene has a character confess a secret the reader already knows. Constraints: the scene must still build tension, add no new plot facts beyond the secret, and fit one page. Which design works?

options.label: Add a new twist at the end of the confession so the reader learns something fresh, which restores suspense to the scene.
Let the confessor lie convincingly instead, so the reader learns a fresh fact about how skilled the deception is.
Summarise the confession in a sentence, since the reader already knows it and extra detail would only slow the page.
Stage it as dramatic irony: the reader waits for the confessor to speak while the listener's reactions raise the stakes.

rubric: Dramatic irony shifts tension from what is said to how and when, and requires no new plot facts.
Distractors add new facts, which breaks a constraint, or drop the scene's tension.
